source.title: Analyzing Hierarchical Structure in Vision Models with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: M. Olson; M. Hinck; Neale Ratzlaff; Chang-Bai Li; Phillip Howard; Vasudev Lal; Shao-Yen Tseng

page_placements.theme: Feature abstraction grows with depth and over pretraining

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how SAE features align with the ImageNet taxonomy, but does not test feature splitting as dictionary size grows, compare features across dictionary sizes, or measure split-family geometry.
record.gate_note: The study trains one SAE size (hidden size 12,288; expansion factor 8) at each DINOv2 layer. It reports taxonomy-alignment results, not a dictionary-size sweep or a test of whether larger-dictionary features partition smaller-dictionary feature inputs.
record.test_reason: The study trains one fixed-size ReLU SAE (hidden size 12,288) per DINOv2 layer and measures how single SAE heads align with the ImageNet/WordNet taxonomy. It never varies dictionary size, matches features across SAEs, measures parent/child firing or decoder geometry, or compares training objectives. Its results therefore do not bear on any version of feature splitting. Hierarchy alignment of individual heads is not V3's nested, geometrically close split families. The text never mentions feature splitting; it only cites SAE work on hierarchical features in LLMs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Per the abstract, the authors conclude that SAEs reveal an implicit encoding of the ImageNet taxonomy in DINOv2, that early-layer class tokens carry little information, and that hierarchical features grow in later layers. The discussion section states that early layers show stronger alignment, which contradicts the paper's own results (Figures 1–2); this is likely an error. The record's limitations paraphrase (one model, ImageNet taxonomy only, SAE redundancy and sparsity artifacts) is accurate.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains fixed-size ReLU SAEs independently at DINOv2 layers; it does not compare dictionary sizes or match features across SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: At DINOv2 layer 36, 90 multi-class SAE heads have ontological coverage 1.0, covering groups such as elasmobranchs, whales, woodwinds and warships.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single fixed-size SAEs on later vision-transformer layers contain latents that each fire on a full higher-level taxonomic category.

fits_no_version.finding: At layer 24, most heads fire on one class or on many dissimilar classes. Head 657 fires on 7 bird species with coverage 0.119.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Taxonomy alignment of SAE latents increases with layer depth in DINOv2.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
record.problems: The study uses a single vision model and focuses on the ImageNet taxonomy. Its reported taxonomy-alignment measurements do not test feature splitting; the authors also note possible redundancy and sparsity-constraint artifacts.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on dictionary-size splitting were reported. Figure 2 also plots taxonomy metrics for layers 28 and 32, but those results do not test splitting or cross-size feature relationships.

untested.parts: All of it: there is no dictionary-size sweep and no test of finer features covering a coarse feature's inputs or lying near its direction.
All of it: there is no splitting test in large models or open SAE releases. One vision model (DINOv2) is used at a single SAE size.
Nested, geometrically close split families. Heads are scored individually against WordNet; there are no families across sizes and no geometry.
All of it: there is no parent-latent failure-to-fire analysis and no size or sparsity variation.
All of it: there is no decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller ones and no count of novel latents.
All of it: there is no comparison of objectives. Sparsity artifacts are only mentioned as a limitation.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation 'discusses' is changed to 'cites_only': the paper never discusses splitting or absorption, and only cites Li et al. on hierarchical SAE features in LLMs. Tranche T6 is confirmed. The rows_left_out declaration of the layer 28 and 32 results is adequate, since those also do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size comparison or test of whether finer features cover a smaller feature's inputs and lie near its direction.
No splitting test at scale or across open SAE releases; the study uses DINOv2 only.
The study measures individual features' alignment with ImageNet taxonomy, not whether split features form nested, geometrically close families.
No parent-child latent firing or change in SAE size or sparsity is tested for absorption.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or assessment of novel latents.
The study notes possible sparsity-constraint artifacts as a limitation, but does not test whether the objective produces splitting or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

relation.reason: The text never mentions feature splitting, absorption or dictionary size, and it does not cite the original sources. It only cites related SAE work, e.g. Li et al. on hierarchical SAE features in LMs. Saying it 'discusses' the finding would overstate its engagement, and of the available categories cites_only is the closest fit.

tranche.reason: The study trains one fixed-size ReLU SAE (hidden 12,288) per DINOv2 layer on the class token and measures how single heads align with the ImageNet/WordNet taxonomy. It never varies dictionary size, matches features across SAEs, or measures parent/child nesting or decoder geometry, so it does not test splitting or V3.

source_check.notes: This is a taxonomy-alignment study with one fixed-size SAE per DINOv2 layer (class token only; the DINOv2 size is not named). It gives no splitting evidence. Its discussion says early layers align more strongly, which contradicts its own Figures 1-2, so this is likely an error.
